newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany heads for EMU shrouded in pessimism.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany heads for EMU shrouded in pessimism.

text.p: The future of Europe's largest economy was shrouded with pessimism on Thursday, as the potential dangers of a single currency and Germany's seemingly unsurmountable jobs crisis deepened the general gloom.

In a key speech on economic and monetary union (EMU), Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer struck at the heart of German worries about Europe's currency plans by warning that fiscal laxity could hurt the stability of the planned euro.

Stressing that "we in Germany are interested in the mark remaining stable and want the euro to be a comparably stable and strong currency," Tietmeyer added: "I hope this view is shared by other European countries."
The single currency, or euro, is scheduled to be launched on January 1, 1999 but 1997 economic data will be used to decide which EU members take part at the start.

Tietmeyer's comments fell amid an atmosphere of growing uncertainty over whether Germany -- once the model pupil in the EMU school -- can manage to rein in its spending sufficiently to meet the tough fiscal targets laid down for EMU entry.

The need to cap spending -- at a time when the population sees Germany's 4.66 million jobless as an urgent and pressing problem -- has led to some social tension in Germany, as people start to fear lasting losses in living standards.
A top pollster said on Thursday the mounting problems had prompted Germans to lose confidence in a predictable future and see themselves living in a time of upheaval and uncertainty.

Renate Koecher of the respected Allensbach Institute told a symposium in Bonn the reaction to heavy job losses and welfare cutbacks was very different to that seen in economic recession four years ago, which had been seen as a passing phase.
"People believe they are living in a time of great upheaval when everyone will have to make big changes," she said.
Many economists believe such an attitude is a healthy step towards the sort of structural change that Germany desperately needs to implement if it is to remain competitive long-term.

Karl Heinrich Oppenlaender of Germany's Ifo economic institute said in Augsburg that persistent inflexibilities in the labour market meant jobless levels would reach 10.9 percent in 1997, up from 10.4 percent last year, and rise further.
Oppenlaender, forecasting 1997 growth of 2.5 percent, said expansion "would have to be three to four percent to do anything about this situation".
Germany was unlikely to achieve its stated goal of halving unemployment by the year 2000, he said, adding: "I cannot imagine this at all."
The failure of the German economy to gather any real momentum in this economic cycle is also a potential barrier to Europe's monetary union starting on time in 1999.
As the deficit and debt targets for EMU compare the budget positions with the year's economic output, solid growth is important to ensure that the targets remain within reach.
Economists at Goldman Sachs said monetary union, while endangered by the risk of slow economic growth, was nonetheless likely to go ahead on time.
"We do think that the most likely event is that a start date of 1999 does get met," Gavyn Davies, chief international economist for Goldman Sachs told a conference in Frankfurt.
But he added such a scenario was "very, very dependent on the growth rate in gross domestic product" in major European nations. Germany and France are seen as essential EMU members.

The bank estimates that a one percentage point shortfall on its GDP growth forecasts would leave both Germany and France with public deficits at around four percent of GDP, far above the three percent figure specified in the Maastricht Treaty that set out the framework for a single currency.
But one positive development for Germany recently has been the fall in its overvalued currency, which helps boost exports.

Tietmeyer said the new exchange rates better matched economic fundamentals, while a second Bundesbank council member, Hans-Juergen Krupp, told a symposium that the dollar's rise from record lows against the mark did not reflect worries about EMU.
The dollar was trading just below 1.69 marks in late European trade, up about 25 percent from its 1995 all-time low.
